title: Rational fixed spaces over algebras and normal-subgroup stability
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], $G$ an affine group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme, def-pc-scheme] of finite type over $k$ [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], $H\subseteq G$ a closed subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], and $V$ a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace] with a rational representation $r:G\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ [def-sc-general-linear-group, after choosing a basis]. Define
$$V^H=\{v\in V:r_B(h)(v\otimes1)=v\otimes1\text{ for every commutative }k\text{-algebra }B\text{ and }h\in H(B)\}.$$
For every commutative $k$-algebra $A$, the natural map $V^H\otimes_k A\to V\otimes_k A$ is injective and identifies its source with
$$\{w\in V\otimes_k A:r_B(h)(w\otimes1)=w\otimes1\text{ for every commutative }A\text{-algebra }B\text{ and }h\in H(B)\}.$$
If $H$ is normal in $G$, every $g\in G(A)$ preserves $V^H\otimes_k A$, and these restrictions define a rational representation of $G$ on $V^H$. The subgroup scheme $H$ acts trivially on that representation. Here $\mathrm{GL}(V)(A)$ means the $A$-linear automorphisms of $V\otimes_k A$; if $V=0$, this is the trivial group scheme $\operatorname{Spec}k$.

source.place: Propositions 4.31 and 4.33, printed p.96, and Lemma 5.15, printed p.102; fixed vectors over every further algebra, followed by normal-subgroup stability.

proof.text: Put $W=V^H$. For each $B,h$, the equation defining $W$ is linear in $v$, so $W$ is a $k$-subspace. We first construct a linear retraction $p:V\to W$. Give $V/W$ a basis by [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-free] and choose in $V$ a lift of each basis vector. Unique finite basis expansions [def-weil-pbc-free-module] extend these lifts to a linear section $s:V/W\to V$ of the quotient $q:V\to V/W$. Then $p(v)=v-s(q(v))$ lies in $W$ and $p(w)=w$ for $w\in W$. In particular $W$ is finite-dimensional: if $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ span $V$, then $p(v_1),\ldots,p(v_n)$ span $W$, by applying $p$ to a spanning expression for $w$. Successively discard any vector in the span of its predecessors in this finite list; the remaining list is an independent spanning family, hence a finite basis of $W$. This includes the empty basis when $W=0$.

source.place: Proposition 4.31, printed p.96: the fixed subspace and its tensor inclusion; explicit linear-algebra preliminaries.

proof.text: Write $\iota:W\hookrightarrow V$. For every $k$-algebra $A$, tensor functoriality [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] gives $(p\otimes1_A)(\iota\otimes1_A)=1_{W\otimes_k A}$, so the natural map is injective. Also choose a $k$-basis $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ of $A$ by [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-free]. Its coordinate maps $\lambda_j:A\to k$ are linear by uniqueness of finite expansions [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. Every element of $M\otimes_k A$, for any $k$-vector space $M$, is $\sum_i m_i\otimes a_i$ with finite support: expand the second factors of a finite sum of pure tensors and collect terms. The tensor universal property gives coefficient maps $E_j^M:M\otimes_k A\to M$, $m\otimes a\mapsto\lambda_j(a)m$, so these coefficients are unique. All reassociations used below are the maps $(v\otimes x)\otimes y\mapsto v\otimes(x\otimes y)$ and their inverses, constructed by the same universal property; their composites fix pure tensors and hence are identities.

source.place: Proposition 4.31, printed p.96: choice of a basis of the scalar algebra and comparison of coefficients.

proof.text: If $w$ lies in the image of $W\otimes_k A$, write $w=\sum_t w_t\otimes b_t$ with $w_t\in W$ using pure-tensor generation [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. For any $A$-algebra $B$ and $h\in H(B)$, its extension is $\sum_t b_t(w_t\otimes1_B)$. Each $w_t\otimes1_B$ is fixed by the definition of $W$, and $r_B(h)$ is $B$-linear, so this sum is fixed. Thus the image is contained in the claimed set of universally fixed vectors.

source.place: Proposition 4.31, printed p.96: the immediate inclusion.

proof.text:
Conversely, let $w\in V\otimes_k A$ satisfy the displayed universal fixed-vector condition and write $w=\sum_i v_i\otimes a_i$ using step 2. Take any commutative $k$-algebra $S$ and $h\in H(S)$. The algebra tensor product [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property] makes $B=S\otimes_k A$ an $A$-algebra by $a\mapsto1\otimes a$. Send $h$ to $h'\in H(B)$ by $s\mapsto s\otimes1$. Naturality of the given morphism $r$ and $B$-linearity imply, in $(V\otimes_k S)\otimes_k A$,
$$0=r_B(h')(w\otimes1_B)-w\otimes1_B=\sum_i\bigl(r_S(h)(v_i\otimes1_S)-v_i\otimes1_S\bigr)\otimes a_i.$$
Apply $E_j^{V\otimes_k S}$ from step 2. It gives $r_S(h)(v_j\otimes1_S)=v_j\otimes1_S$. Since $S,h$ were arbitrary, every $v_j$ belongs to $W$, and $w$ is in the image of $W\otimes_k A$. The reassociations and coefficient maps here use [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. No density of field-valued points is used.

source.place: Proposition 4.31, printed p.96: its basis-coefficient argument, applied to the restricted representation of H.

proof.text:
Assume $H$ is normal. Let $g\in G(A)$ and $w\in W\otimes_k A$, viewed in $V\otimes_k A$ by step 2. For any $A$-algebra $B$ and $h\in H(B)$, normality [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup] gives $g_B^{-1}hg_B\in H(B)$. By steps 3--4 and the representation law,
$$r_B(h)r_B(g_B)w_B=r_B(g_B)r_B(g_B^{-1}hg_B)w_B=r_B(g_B)w_B.$$
Thus step 4 puts $r_A(g)w$ in $W\otimes_k A$. Applying the same argument to $g^{-1}$ shows that the restriction $T_A(g)$ is an $A$-linear automorphism. The restrictions commute with $A\to B$: their composites with the injective map $W\otimes_k B\hookrightarrow V\otimes_k B$ agree by naturality of $r$, hence they agree. Their products and identities likewise agree after this injection.

source.place: Lemma 5.15, printed p.102: the explicit conjugation calculation and its consequence using Proposition 4.31.

proof.text: To check rationality, write $G=\operatorname{Spec}C$, possible since $G$ is affine [def-pc-scheme]. The identity $C\to C$ represents a universal point $u\in G(C)$ by [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. If $d=\dim_kW>0$, use the finite basis of $W$ from step 1. The automorphism $T_C(u)$ is an invertible $d\times d$ matrix over $C$, hence a $C$-point of $\mathrm{GL}_{d,k}$ by [def-sc-general-linear-group]. A $C$-point is precisely a $k$-morphism $r_W:G=\operatorname{Spec}C\to\mathrm{GL}_{d,k}$. For every $k$-algebra $A$, a point $g\in G(A)$ corresponds to a $k$-algebra map $f:C\to A$. The $A$-point of $r_W$ at $g$ is the matrix obtained by applying $f$ to $T_C(u)$. By the naturality proved in step 5 this is exactly $T_A(g)$. Thus this actual scheme morphism realizes all the restrictions simultaneously, including over algebras with nilpotents.

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed pp.83--84 (universal element and its representing matrix), and Lemma 5.15, printed p.102 (restricted rational action).

proof.text: The morphism $r_W$ respects multiplication, as can be checked on each affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}D$ of $G\times_kG$ [def-pc-scheme]. Its two projections define $g_1,g_2\in G(D)$. The two multiplication composites on $U$ have the matrices $T_D(g_1g_2)$ and $T_D(g_1)T_D(g_2)$, equal by step 5, so they are the same morphism by [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Equality on this open cover is equality of the scheme morphisms (both the underlying maps and the sheaf maps agree on each open). The identity is preserved by $T_k(1)=1$. These are the group-scheme homomorphism diagrams [def-sc-group-scheme], so $r_W$ is a rational representation. If $h\in H(A)$, step 3 with $B=A$ gives $T_A(h)w=w$ for every $w\in W\otimes_k A$, so $H$ acts trivially. The corresponding morphisms on $H$ agree by the same test on its affine opens. If $W=0$, use the unique map $G\to\operatorname{Spec}k$; its action on $0\otimes_k A=0$ is the unique automorphism, so all assertions hold.

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed pp.83--84; Propositions 4.31 and 4.33, printed p.96; Lemma 5.15, printed p.102: group law and trivial H-action on the restricted representation.

proof_origin.place: Proposition 4.31, printed p.96; Lemma 5.15, printed p.102; Remark 4.1, printed pp.83--84, for the universal matrix description of rationality.
